newsitem.title: SPAIN: Squeezed Spanish banks resist matching BoS cut.
newsitem.headline: Squeezed Spanish banks resist matching BoS cut.

text.p: One day after the Bank of Spain reduced its official interest rate by 50 basis points to 6.75 percent, most top Spanish banks had not followed suit and reduced borrowing costs.
Analysts said on Friday they doubted this would change.
Low and rigid demand for loans, the halving of interest margins in recent years and a declining trend in money market rates are leaving commercial banks squeezed.
"Banks could cut their rates in the coming days. ..But up to now, they seem happier not doing it," said Miguel Artola, banking analyst with Schroeder in Madrid.

"They seem convinced they will make more money by not lowering rates because loan demand is low and rigid, and they would not get enough loans to compensate for the loss in income if they reduced the price," he said.
Yesterday Bankinter was the only top retail bank to follow the Bank of Spain's lead.
"We are not ruling out the possibility of lowering our rates in coming days," a source in Banco Bilbao Vizcaya said.
"It's not like it used to be. Now the interest rate trend is clearer, and the banks can wait instead of lowering right after the central bank announcement," the source said.
This year, the Bank of Spain has cut its key money market rate six times, bringing it to 6.75 percent from nine percent.
A shift in the composition of banks' balance sheets also has to be taken into account because much of their new business is not directly affected by an official rate cut, analysts said.
Banks now have more indexed loans than in the past, especially on the mortgage side where from the second year the rate is linked to the Madrid interbank offered rate (Mibor).
"The prime rate is not the rate which is really used," said Alejandro Ruyra, banking analyst at AB Asesores in Madrid.
The customer yield spread, or the average revenue from loans less the average cost of deposits, has declined steadily in the past three years.
The spread came down 47 percent to 5.1 percent last month from 7.1 percent at the beginning of 1993, Ruyra said, adding that he expected a further 12-percent decline to 4.6 percent.
"They have little room to cut the deposit rates, mainly because many are already very low," Artola said.
And with new official interest rate cuts seen in coming months, commercial banks will try to compete in other areas.
"In recent years, banks have tried to compete more on product differentiation, offering, for example, more service to clients rather than competing on prices," Ruyra added.
Some analysts added that banks' resistance to cutting their rates could curb a pick-up in economic growth, analysts said.
